questions.question: Sarah, you ran the numbers on Fielding's big speech — 'I believe in teaching people to be individuals' — and what you found was basically that the guy preaching openness and connection speaks like a government memo. Can you just tell us what that gap looks like when you actually measure it?
questions.intent: Open with the most counterintuitive finding to grab listeners — the quantitative case that Fielding's language betrays his stated values sets up everything that follows

questions.question: Rebecca, you came at the same speech from a completely different angle and ended up somewhere related but weirder — you said the emphatic 'I do believe' is actually a sign of fragility, not confidence. That the grammar is bracing for a hit. Which means Forster is encoding doubt at the exact moment his character is making his most famous declaration of faith. How does that work?
questions.intent: Draw out the counter-presuppositional finding and complicate any instinct to read Fielding as the novel's moral centre — also sets up the 'grammar of doubt' thesis that runs through all three passages

questions.question: Elena, there's a moment in chapter 26 where Fielding is telling Aziz 'my belief is that McBryde exorcised you' — and he sounds like he's being generous, reconciliatory, big-hearted. But Rebecca flagged a parenthetical in there — 'in hope you would make some slip' — where Fielding basically confesses mid-sentence that he was listening for Aziz to incriminate himself. You've argued this passage isn't really about exorcism at all. What is it about?
questions.intent: Force a reading of the most dramatically uncomfortable passage — Fielding's embedded confession — and test Elena's claim that the three passages represent contradictory theories of what language is for

questions.question: You've called the whole novel a failed sonata — Forster builds toward resolution and then at the last moment substitutes consolation for it, like landing on the wrong chord. The third passage, Aziz turning to literature because facts are ugly — you're saying that's not Forster affirming the power of culture, it's Forster documenting a retreat. But isn't that quite a dark reading of what Forster thought he was doing?
questions.intent: Provoke Elena on the 'failed sonata' thesis and whether Forster's consolation is a structural failure or a deliberate honesty — designed to draw in Rebecca on the sentimental vs. defensive reading of the solace line

questions.question: Rebecca, all three of you have landed on roughly the same place from very different directions — that this novel's most articulate characters are hedging, defending, retreating, confessing bad faith. But A Passage to India is still taught as a classic of liberal humanist optimism. Are we all wrong, or is the novel smarter than its reputation?
questions.intent: Synthesise the convergence across methods into a direct provocation about the novel's canonical status — designed as a round-table closer that lets all three experts respond

steering_notes: The energy here should be three people who've all pulled on the same thread from different ends and are slightly surprised to find they're holding the same rope. Don't let it become a methodological debate — keep redirecting to what each finding means for how we read the novel. The Fielding-as-memo finding (Sarah) and the emphatic-do-as-fragility finding (Rebecca) are the two best opening provocations; get both on the table before moving to chapter 26. Elena's failed-sonata thesis is the biggest structural claim and should land last in this segment, as a frame for everything that follows.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's register analysis (Fielding speaks like a bureaucratic document) directly contradicts Elena's dependency-structure point in a productive way — Elena says the colonial hierarchy is built into the grammar's agent-object structure, Sarah says the problem runs deeper into lexical register; push them to agree or disagree on whether that's the same finding

Rebecca's reading of the solace passage as structurally defensive (literature as consolation that might be taken away) is in direct tension with Elena's survival-strategy reading — Elena thinks the comfort reading misses the institutional pressure, Rebecca thinks the grammar makes the same point through syntax; host should surface this as a near-agreement that conceals a real difference

The parenthetical confession in c26:p29 is flagged by both Rebecca and Sarah as the most structurally significant moment in that passage — Rebecca via counter-presupposition, Sarah via disfluency repair pattern — and both are pushing back against letting the word 'exorcised' dominate; this convergence should be named explicitly on air

segment_name: The Machinery of Empire: Law, Institution, and the Raj

questions.question: You've looked very closely at McBryde's cross-examination in Chapter 24 — and you found something almost paradoxical: that the legal language is unusually thin, low on content, almost hollow. So what is it actually doing? What is all that legal scaffolding scaffolding *around*?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to land her strongest take — that the elaborate legal register is a vehicle for a single coercive proposition — and set up the disagreement about whether this is syntax *enacting* ideology or syntax *describing* it

questions.question: Rebecca, you've said something that I want to push on — that the crack in the machinery, the thing that lets Adela escape, is actually built into McBryde's own sentence. 'I suggest to you that the prisoner followed you.' That phrase is doing something very specific. What does it do to Adela as a grammatical object in that sentence — and how does that same sentence give her a way out?
questions.intent: Draw out Rebecca's strongest take on prosecutorial grammar as simultaneously coercive and structurally flawed — the flaw is in the formula itself

questions.question: Elena, you've described the courtroom as a failed fugue — Das is forced to mute his own instrument, McBryde collapses everything into one repeated line. But Sarah would say that's not a musical metaphor, that's just what the dependency parse shows us: one proposition, repeated. Are you two actually saying the same thing in different languages, or is there a real disagreement there about what Forster is doing?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Elena's musical-structural reading and Sarah's computational one — find whether they converge or genuinely diverge on the Das moment specifically

questions.question: You've suggested that the collar-stud sentence in Chapter 8 recruits the reader into Ronny's logic before we can object — that the cadence pulls us along. But Rebecca is arguing there's no formal ironic signal in that passage at all on a cold read, that the irony is retrospective. So is Forster letting us off the hook, or is he making us complicit? And does that distinction matter?
questions.intent: Pit Elena's reader-complicity argument against Rebecca's cold-read structural argument — this is the segment's richest disagreement and should generate genuine friction

questions.question: There's a line at the end of the novel — 'it's nobody's India' — that all three of you have circled. Rebecca, you said Forster lets 'nobody' be a real answer, not a temporary one. Sarah thinks the pragmatics of that sentence are coercive — that Fielding can only claim India belongs to nobody before he's relinquished his own claim on it. Who's right? Is 'nobody's India' a moment of honesty, or is it one more colonial sentence wearing the clothes of resignation?
questions.intent: Close the segment on the sharpest possible disagreement — Rebecca's reading of genuine openness versus Sarah's pragmatic critique of Fielding's authority to make the claim at all — with Elena able to offer the musical reading of hollow major as a third option

steering_notes: This segment has real heat in it — let it run. The richest fault line is between Sarah's position that the ideology is in the sentence architecture itself and Elena's that Forster makes the reader participate in it rhythmically: Rebecca sits between them, insisting the irony is structural but retrospective, not built in. Don't resolve that triangle. The Das moment is the best single image in the segment — try to get all three experts on it before moving on. If energy dips, the collar-stud passage is the reliable ignition point: everyone has a strong read and they genuinely conflict.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah vs Elena on the collar-stud cadence: Sarah says the sentence parse convicts Ronny before the narrator speaks; Elena says the cadence recruits the reader into Ronny's logic before objection is possible — these look compatible but disagree on where the reader is positioned relative to the ideology

Rebecca vs Sarah on the nature of exposure: Rebecca frames Forster as exposing the Raj through the grammar's own flaw; Sarah argues the exposure is not in any authorial gloss but is the architecture itself — no Forster 'behind' the sentence, just the sentence

Elena vs Sarah on 'nobody's India': Elena reads the Fielding-Aziz exchange as a theme-and-variation pair with emotional register shift; Sarah argues the pragmatics are coercive regardless of emotional register — sentiment analysis cannot track authority conditions on assertions

All three on Das hiding his face in papers: Rebecca sees a real-time split between official and human sentence; Elena sees the fugue's breakdown; Sarah sees institutionally constrained agency in the grammar — this is the segment's best convergence point and worth slowing down for

segment_name: Reading Aziz: Dignity Before the Fall

questions.question: Rebecca, you've been staring at about a hundred words in that kindness speech — Aziz saying 'kindness, more kindness, and even after that more kindness' — and you told me before we started that something happens to the word 'kindness' the moment it leaves Aziz's mouth and enters Fielding's head. What actually happens to it?
questions.intent: Get Rebecca to land her strongest take — the syntactic shift from Aziz's aspiration to Fielding's resource — early and vividly, and set up the core tension of the segment

questions.question: Sarah, you actually ran the numbers on who's speaking more richly in these passages, and the answer surprised me. Because the expected story here is Aziz as the wounded colonial subject — diminished, pleading. But that's not what you found, is it?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to complicate the postcolonial victimhood reading with her TTR and lexical richness data, creating productive friction with Rebecca's reading of Aziz in the 'rhetoric of need'

questions.question: Rebecca, I want to push on that, because you said Forster may have unconsciously handed Aziz the rhetoric of need and Fielding the rhetoric of authority — even in a passage that's explicitly mocking imperial authority. But Sarah's just told us Aziz's language is actually more alive by the numbers. Can those two things both be true at the same time?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Rebecca's structural-asymmetry reading and Sarah's lexical-richness finding — this is the segment's central disagreement and should produce the best radio

questions.question: Sarah, you flagged that passage in chapter sixteen — Aziz rattling off 'a penny saved is a penny earned, a stitch in time saves nine' and then 'the British Empire rests on them' — as the most linguistically violent moment in the whole set. That's a strong claim. What's the violence, exactly, and where does it live in the sentence?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to deliver her 'three-node dependency structure' insight without using the jargon — make her translate it into something a listener can feel — and open up the question of whether the proverbs passage is straightforwardly ironic

questions.question: Rebecca, you said something in our pre-conversation that's been nagging at me — that the scene where Fielding sits there thinking 'was that really all that the queer nation needed?' isn't Fielding opening his mind to Aziz's worldview. You called it something like intellectual colonization dressed as openness. Can you say what you meant by that?
questions.intent: Get Rebecca to articulate her reading of Fielding's free indirect discourse as appropriation, which should provoke Sarah on where exactly the FID boundary sits and what it means

steering_notes: The central productive tension in this segment is between Sarah's finding that Aziz is linguistically more vital than Fielding and Rebecca's finding that the structure of the kindness speech encodes a rhetoric of need. Don't let either expert simply win — the best outcome is both readings standing simultaneously and the guests having to explain how that's possible. Keep pushing toward the concrete: when either guest goes abstract, ask them to find the line. Elena's key points were not available so lean into Sarah and Rebecca carrying the argument. If energy dips, go back to the proverbs passage — 'the British Empire rests on them' is a sentence almost anyone can have a strong reaction to.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's lexical richness finding directly challenges Rebecca's 'rhetoric of need' framing — after Sarah lands the TTR point, immediately invite Rebecca to respond rather than moving on

Rebecca's reading of the FID passage as Fielding quietly appropriating Aziz's conviction should be put to Sarah, who has a precise grammatical account of where the FID boundary actually sits — these two readings may complement or contest each other

The proverbs passage is where both experts have strong takes that approach from different angles: Sarah sees syntactic hollowness, Rebecca sees performed benevolence — get them to work on that passage together rather than sequentially

segment_name: The Caves as Rupture: What Adela Hears and Doesn't Hear

questions.question: Sarah, you said the cave isn't actually the rupture — that it's already happened before Adela goes anywhere near the Marabar Hills, and it happened in a single word. The word 'error,' applied to something Forster has just told us is the truth. What does that do to everything that comes after?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to deliver her strongest take — the grammatical lie in c14:p78 as rehearsal for the novel's epistemological collapse — and set up the central disagreement about where the rupture actually lives

questions.question: Elena, you've been saying something that sounds similar but I think is actually different — that the rupture is in the grammar of c14, in the way the sentence performs the scattering it describes, the dash and the delayed predicate. So are you and Sarah agreeing that the rupture is pre-cave, or are you actually pointing at different things?
questions.intent: Force a productive distinction between Sarah's lexical-semantic argument (the word 'error') and Elena's syntactic-performative argument (the dash-fermata enacting the scatter) — two pre-cave ruptures that may not be the same rupture

questions.question: Rebecca, you described the caves as a null result that Forster refuses to label as one — everyone including Forster's own prose keeps trying to convert the emptiness into a finding. But Sarah and Elena are both saying the emptiness was manufactured before the caves, in the grammar of chapter fourteen. Does that change your reading, or does the null result hold regardless of when it was planted?
questions.intent: Create a three-way tension: Sarah's grammatical lie, Elena's formal blank protocol, and Rebecca's null-result framing — push Rebecca to either synthesize or contest the pre-cave argument

questions.question: Elena, you called the caves a blank protocol — a file whose index entry exists but whose content is withheld, and everything that follows is procedural noise around the gap. That's a striking structural claim. But Rebecca's point is that Forster's prose can't actually stay empty — it keeps generating meaning even when the plot demands the void. Is the blank protocol really holding, or is Forster's syntax constantly breaking its own silence?
questions.intent: Pit Elena's structural-formalist argument (the blank as intentional architecture) against Rebecca's observation that the prose itself refuses to honour the blankness — rich disagreement about authorial control vs. textual self-betrayal

questions.question: Rebecca, you said there's a passage — 'Perhaps life is a mystery, not a muddle; they could not tell' — where the same phrase, 'they could not tell,' covers questions of completely different scale, cosmological and local, as if uncertainty doesn't scale with the size of the question. Sarah, you've flagged the same passage as evidence that the grammar has been trained to distrust certainty. Are you reading that as the same move, or is one of you describing a feature and the other a flaw?
questions.intent: Bring both Sarah and Rebecca to the c29:p16 passage simultaneously — Sarah sees trained grammatical distrust, Rebecca sees deliberate equivalence of scales — and let them argue about whether Forster is in control of what the sentence is doing

steering_notes: The productive engine of this segment is the question of location: where is the rupture? Sarah says a single word in c14, Elena says the syntactic structure of c14 (slightly different claim), Rebecca says the rupture is everywhere and nowhere because the null result was never labelled. Don't let this become three separate presentations — keep pushing them to address each other's specific formulations. The 'error' word is the sharpest concrete object to keep returning to when discussion goes abstract. If energy dips, ask someone to read the desert flower sentence aloud and then ask why three people with completely different methods all end up at the same sentence.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's claim that 'error' is a grammatical lie directly sets up Elena's claim that the syntax of the same passage performs the rupture — these are complementary but not identical, and the distinction is worth making audible

Rebecca's null-result framing nominally agrees with Elena's blank-protocol framing but Rebecca's additional claim — that Forster's prose breaks its own silence — is a direct challenge to Elena's structural control argument

Sarah's argument that Aziz's free indirect discourse in c13 is a colonial power asymmetry embedded in syntax sits in productive tension with Elena's insistence that grammatical incompleteness must be examined as formal structure before political content — they're describing the same sentences with incompatible priorities

segment_name: The Trial and Its Aftermath: Justice Unmade

questions.question: Elena, you've described the Marabar as a development section that refuses to develop — it destroys thematic material rather than transforming it. But I want to ask about the actual sentence that delivers the verdict. You said 'boum' arrives after 44 syllables of what you called 'architectural sentence weight.' What does that feel like, physically, when you read it? What does Forster do to us in that moment?
questions.intent: Get Elena to perform the 44:1 cadential collapse reading live, setting up the 'boum' passage for quotation and creating a shared anchor point all three experts can respond to

questions.question: Rebecca, you'd push back on anyone calling 'boum' mystical silence or apophatic theology — you've said it's better modeled as confusion noise, carrying energy but no information. But Elena just described it as a rhythmic collapse into silence, and Sarah's been saying it's the most information-dense word in the whole passage. So who's right? Is 'boum' the sound of too much meaning or none at all?
questions.intent: Force a three-way collision on the central interpretive crux — noise vs. silence vs. information paradox — using the experts' directly contradictory pre-interview positions

questions.question: Sarah, you made this striking claim that Mrs. Moore's breakdown isn't just bleak content — it's a breakdown of the narrator register itself, that Forster literally changed the grammar and syntax when he entered her consciousness. Can you read us the passage and point to where you see that happening? What's the tell?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to quote the Mrs. Moore passage and identify the specific syntactic features, grounding the abstract register-shift claim in the actual words on the page

questions.question: Rebecca, you said the friendship passage in chapter eleven — Aziz drifting into that vision of the eternal garden — is only available because Aziz has just performed an act of social hierarchy, placed Fielding below himself. That feels almost cruel. Are you saying the most beautiful moment in the novel is structurally tainted? That the brotherhood is real but the conditions for it are not?
questions.intent: Draw out Rebecca's most uncomfortable finding about the asymmetry of the friendship vision and provoke Elena and Sarah on whether formal beauty can be separated from the conditions that enable it

questions.question: Elena, you said Aziz's Islamic paradise — the ninety-nine attributes inscribed in the domes — survives the Marabar echo precisely because it's non-narrative, geometric, not a story that can be collapsed into noise. But Rebecca's just told us that vision is built on a hierarchy, and Sarah would say the register of that passage is detectably Aziz's interiority, not some eternal formal system. So is the paradise real, or is it Aziz's version of 'boum' — a beautiful word that fills the void?
questions.intent: Create a closing synthesis question that forces all three to reckon with whether Forster offers any genuine alternative to the Marabar's negation, or whether all the passages end in the same place

steering_notes: This segment has a natural arc: establish what 'boum' does (Q1), fight about what it means (Q2), ground it in the actual text (Q3), interrogate the novel's only apparent affirmation (Q4), then force a reckoning with whether anything survives (Q5). The three experts have genuinely incompatible positions on 'boum' — noise, silence, information paradox — and that's the engine. Don't let anyone retreat to methodology; keep pushing them back to the words on the page. If the conversation stalls, the 'sinister feature' passage is a useful reset — all three want to quote it and have different readings of it.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's information-theoretic claim that 'boum' is maximum-surprise (most information-dense) directly contradicts Rebecca's null-result/confusion-noise model — the same word cannot simultaneously carry maximum information and zero information, and the experts should be asked to resolve this tension explicitly

Rebecca's finding that the eternal garden vision is enabled by Aziz's act of social hierarchy directly undercuts Elena's reading of Islamic geometric inscription as a formally durable alternative system — if the access condition is hierarchy, the form is not neutral

Elena's claim that the Caves destroy thematic material rather than transform it is in productive tension with Sarah's finding that the narrator-register shift is a kind of transformation — the form isn't destroyed, it's cannibalized into a new mode, which is not the same as silence

questions.question: So the 'India a nation!' passage — the one with Guatemala and Belgium — most readers just hear that as Forster being wry about nationalism. But you're saying we can't even assign that voice to Forster, or to the narrator, until we figure out whether it's actually Fielding thinking it. Walk us through what's at stake there, because if you're right, it changes who we're prosecuting.
questions.intent: Get Sarah to lay out the FID attribution argument for 'India a nation!' and establish the syntactic case for Fielding as speaker — setting up the direct contradiction with Rebecca's point that 'Fielding mocked again' comes *after* the exclamations, which destabilises the attribution.

questions.question: Rebecca, you've flagged something that I think blows a hole in that reading — the phrase 'Fielding mocked again' appears *after* the fireworks, which means the sarcasm might already be the narrator's before Fielding gets credit for it. So is Fielding even in that passage in the way we think he is?
questions.intent: Surface the direct contradiction with Sarah — Rebecca's sequencing argument undermines the stable FID attribution Sarah relies on. Should provoke Sarah to defend or refine. Also sets up Elena's polytonal framing as a possible resolution to the stand-off.

questions.question: Elena, you've described that same passage — Fielding's mockery, Aziz's rage — as polytonal, two voices that Forster refuses to resolve. Is that actually a way out of the argument Sarah and Rebecca are having, or does it just reframe the problem? Because I want to know: does Forster *not resolve it* because he can't, or because he's decided resolution would be dishonest?
questions.intent: Push Elena to commit to whether the polytonal reading is a formal achievement or a structural evasion — drawing out her strongest claim that irresolution is compositionally deliberate, and forcing her to take a position on Forster's intention rather than just describing the texture.

questions.question: Rebecca, you've tracked passive constructions as a kind of God-detector across the novel — agency disappears when transcendence arrives. But then you hit the 'heart of a cloud' sentence in the Mau chapter and you've said the method just breaks down. Is that a problem, or is Forster actually telling us something by defeating the instrument at exactly that moment?
questions.intent: Draw out Rebecca's 'null result as data' argument and get her to defend the idea that analytical breakdown is itself meaningful — sets up a clash with Sarah, who reads the same sentence as documenting epistemic failure rather than enacting transcendence, and with Elena, whose negation-ratio analysis claims to *penetrate* the blur rather than be defeated by it.

questions.question: Sarah, you've called the engagement sentence — 'He assented, and they became engaged to be married in consequence' — one of the most quietly devastating lines in the book. The phrase 'in consequence' is doing something really strange there. What is it doing, exactly?
questions.intent: Get Sarah to unpack the presupposition trigger and affective resignation encoded in 'in consequence' — Elena will want to jump in with the colonial administrative register reading, creating a moment where the linguistic and the historical-formal readings meet or clash.

steering_notes: The productive tension in this segment runs between Sarah's attribution-first discipline (you can't assign political meaning until you know whose voice it is), Rebecca's structural-pattern approach (the grammar tracks something systematic regardless of attribution), and Elena's formal analogy (the novel's irresolution is engineered, not evasive). The Guatemala/Belgium passage is the live wire — return to it after each expert has staked a position, because the three readings are genuinely incompatible and the audience will feel that. Don't let Elena's musical analogies become decorative; push her to say what Forster gains by withholding resolution. The 'heart of a cloud' sentence is a useful reset point mid-segment — everyone has something to say about it and it's short enough to quote on air.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's FID attribution argument for 'India a nation!' directly contradicts Rebecca's sequencing point ('Fielding mocked again' comes after) — get them to address each other's evidence, not just restate their own position.

Rebecca's 'null result' in the Mau chapter (method breaks down at transcendence) conflicts with Elena's negation-ratio analysis of the same passage (which claims to measure the blur precisely) — these two claims cannot both be true and the clash is worth surfacing explicitly.

Elena's polytonal reading of c37:p27 (neither voice cancels the other) could either resolve or deepen the Sarah/Rebecca stand-off on FID attribution — ask Elena directly whether her framing makes the attribution question moot or more urgent.

All three experts quote the engagement sentence but read it differently: Sarah hears presupposed resignation, Elena hears colonial administrative register, Rebecca hears encoded human agency in subordinate clauses — a three-way collision worth manufacturing deliberately near the end of the segment.

segment_name: Closing: The Novel's Last Word on Connection

questions.question: Elena, you said the three-part structure is a sonata with a failed recapitulation — that the cave passage tells us in advance that Temple can't resolve anything. But if Forster knew it couldn't resolve, why build the architecture that promises it will? Is he setting us up to feel the failure, or did he write himself into a corner he couldn't get out of?
questions.intent: Get Elena to commit to the failed-form argument at full strength, and open the door for Rebecca to push back on whether 'failure' is the right frame versus 'convergence result'

questions.question: Sarah, you found two incompatible grammars running in parallel — the caves all aperture, Fielding all closure — and you're saying that's the novel's actual argument, not just its mood. So when Forster writes that sentence about the two flames approaching and striving to unite but not being able to — can you read us that passage and tell us what the grammar is actually doing there, at the sentence level?
questions.intent: Get the c12:p3 flame passage read aloud and Sarah's analysis of it as periodic sentence enacting separation; sets up direct comparison with Elena's musical deceptive-cadence reading of the same passage

questions.question: Rebecca, you called the famous closing deferral — 'No, not yet, no, not there' — not a lament but a convergence result. That's a cold way to put it, and you said yourself it sounds cold. But does calling it a convergence result actually make it more heartbreaking, or does it let Forster — and us — off the hook emotionally?
questions.intent: Force Rebecca to defend the analytical framing against the emotional stakes; create tension between her systems-level reading and Elena's 'rest not resolution' argument

questions.question: Elena, you said Fielding's equanimity — his 'I really don't mind' — is a privilege of power, not wisdom. That he can afford not to mind because his colonial role lets him exit intimacy without cost. But Sarah found that his grammar is closed and complete, that the sentence itself enacts retreat. Does the form of that sentence change your reading — or does form just make the rationalization more elegant?
questions.intent: Direct cross-engagement between Elena and Sarah on c11:p21; tests whether grammatical evidence supports or complicates the institutional-power reading

questions.question: Rebecca, you flagged that 'With so emotional a people' might be Fielding's free indirect discourse — not Forster endorsing Orientalism but Forster letting Fielding hang himself with it. Sarah thinks the generalizing form is itself the critique because Forster does it to every group. Are those actually the same argument, or are you two disagreeing about who's doing the judging — the character or the author?
questions.intent: Surface the sharpest methodological and interpretive disagreement in the room; force clarity on whether FID attribution and pattern-of-usage arguments are compatible or competing explanations

steering_notes: This segment should build from form outward to meaning — start with Elena's structural argument, move through the specific passages, and end on the FID/Orientalism question which is genuinely unresolved and will generate heat. Don't let anyone retreat to pure method; keep pushing toward what the findings mean for how we feel reading the ending. The two-flames passage should be read aloud at least once — make sure that happens in question 2. If the convergence-result vs. rest-not-resolution debate stalls, push both Rebecca and Elena on whether their framings are compatible or one of them has to be wrong.
cross_engagement_targets: Sarah's two-incompatible-grammars claim vs. Elena's deceptive-cadence reading of the same flame sentence in c12:p3 — they may be describing the same phenomenon in different vocabularies, or they may actually disagree about whether the sentence performs separation or withholds resolution

Elena's institutional-power reading of Fielding's equanimity directly challenges Rebecca's reading of the same sentence as a conditional with no pathway to grief — Elena says the form is a rationalization, Rebecca says the form reveals a psychological limit; one of them has to give ground

Rebecca's FID argument and Sarah's pattern-of-usage argument about 'so emotional a people' look compatible on the surface but imply different things about authorial control — Rebecca needs the irony to be local and attributed, Sarah needs it to be structural and distributed across the whole novel
